stem: You are the psychiatry registrar assessing a 31-year-old man with a 6-year illness. He has had 3 manic episodes with mood-congruent grandiose delusions, each followed by 6 to 12 months of residual auditory hallucinations and persecutory delusions without significant mood symptoms. Between episodes he has not returned to premorbid function and has continuing negative symptoms. His family history is significant for both bipolar and schizophrenia. He is currently on no medication after self-discontinuation 6 months ago.

data_table.Examination: Flat affect, third person auditory hallucinations, persecutory delusions, no current mania, no current depression
data_table.Investigations: FBC, U&E, LFTs, TSH, urine drug screen normal; CT brain no acute change

lead_in: Which DSM-5-TR diagnosis is most consistent with this clinical course?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features and a current episode in partial remission with residual symptoms
options.rationale: Bipolar I requires psychotic features to be confined to mood episodes; psychosis persisting for 6 to 12 months without prominent mood disturbance does not fit. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Schizophrenia, paranoid type, with secondary mood episodes related to illness burden rather than primary affective disorder
options.rationale: Paranoid type is no longer a DSM-5-TR specifier; full manic episodes with mood-congruent psychosis weigh against primary schizophrenia. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, with mood episodes and at least 2 weeks of psychosis without prominent mood symptoms
options.rationale: Schizoaffective disorder requires at least 2 weeks of psychotic symptoms without major mood episode and mood episodes for a substantial portion of total illness; this case fits the bipolar subtype. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Schizophreniform disorder evolving towards schizophrenia, with affective symptoms attributable to chronic illness burden
options.rationale: Schizophreniform is by definition shorter than 6 months and does not feature full manic episodes; ill-fitting given the 6-year course. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with persistent inter-episode psychotic symptoms and high familial loading for both bipolar and schizophrenia
options.rationale: Persistent inter-episode psychosis crosses the boundary out of bipolar disorder into schizoaffective territory; the diagnosis should reflect the longitudinal course. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: DSM-5-TR distinguishes schizoaffective disorder from bipolar I with psychotic features by the longitudinal pattern of psychosis. Schizoaffective requires at least 2 weeks of psychotic symptoms without prominent mood disturbance during the lifetime course, plus mood episodes for a substantial portion of total illness duration. The bipolar subtype includes manic episodes; the depressive subtype is restricted to major depressive episodes. Treatment usually combines an antipsychotic with a mood stabiliser.
key_points: Schizoaffective requires at least 2 weeks of psychosis without mood symptoms
Mood episodes must occur during a substantial portion of total illness
Bipolar subtype includes mania; depressive subtype is MDE-only
Treatment combines antipsychotic plus mood stabiliser
explanation.pearls: Substantial portion is not numerically defined in DSM-5-TR but typically interpreted as at least one third to half of total active illness time.

stem: You are the GP reviewing a 26-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder diagnosed 18 months ago. She has chronic suicidal ideation, intermittent self-harm by superficial cutting, intense unstable relationships and emotional dysregulation. She is not currently suicidal at this consultation but has cut twice in the last week to manage emotional distress. She has been on sertraline 200 mg for 12 months with no clear benefit. She is engaged with her GP and is willing to try further interventions. There is no acute psychosis.

data_table.Examination: Settled today; superficial linear cuts on left forearm at varied stages of healing; no infection; HEADSS reveals no acute risk
data_table.Investigations: PHQ-9 score 18, K10 score 32; FBC, TFT, UEC, LFT normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Switch sertraline to fluoxetine and re-titrate over 8 weeks; defer psychological therapy until antidepressant response is established
options.rationale: Switching antidepressants without first addressing underlying personality structure is unlikely to help; structured psychotherapy is the cornerstone. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Add lamotrigine 200 mg daily as a mood stabiliser to address affective instability and recurrent superficial self-harm episodes
options.rationale: Lamotrigine and other mood stabilisers do not show consistent benefit in BPD core symptoms; structured psychotherapy is the recommended first-line. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Admit to inpatient psychiatric unit for prolonged stabilisation and observation; defer outpatient therapy until safety is fully established
options.rationale: Prolonged inpatient admission can worsen BPD by regression, dependence and reinforcement of crisis behaviour; short focused admissions only when immediate safety requires. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Refer for structured psychotherapy (dialectical behaviour therapy or mentalisation-based therapy); review medication once therapy is established
options.rationale: Structured psychotherapy (DBT or MBT) is first-line evidence-based treatment for BPD; pharmacotherapy is adjunctive at best and is reviewed once therapy is in place. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Commence olanzapine 5 mg daily for emotional dysregulation; review weight and full metabolic parameters every 3 months on therapy
options.rationale: Antipsychotics in BPD are used cautiously and short-term for transient psychotic features or severe affective storms; not first-line for chronic dysregulation. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline)

explanation.summary: Borderline personality disorder is managed by structured evidence-based psychotherapy: dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT), mentalisation-based therapy (MBT), schema-focused therapy or transference-focused psychotherapy. Australian NHMRC guidance places these as first-line. Pharmacotherapy is adjunctive only: short-term symptom-targeted use of antipsychotics for psychotic features, mood stabilisers for affective storms, antidepressants for comorbid depression. Avoid polypharmacy. Prolonged inpatient admission can worsen outcomes; brief focused admissions only when immediate safety requires. Co-design care plans and crisis plans with the patient.
key_points: DBT or MBT is first-line evidence-based treatment
Pharmacotherapy is adjunctive only; avoid polypharmacy
Brief targeted admissions, not prolonged stays
Co-designed crisis and care plans
explanation.pearls: Validation of distress without endorsing self-harm and clear consistent limit-setting reduces splitting and crisis escalation in primary care.

stem: You are the GP seeing a 24-year-old woman three months after she was hit by a car as a pedestrian. She continues to have nightmares of the crash, avoids walking on roads, has hypervigilance at intersections and intrusive memories several times a day. She has not been able to return to her university course. She has no past psychiatric history and is not on any medications. She is sexually active and uses a copper IUD for contraception. She drinks no alcohol.

data_table.Examination: Tearful, well-groomed, normal cognition, no thought disorder, denies self-harm or suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: PCL-5 score 52 out of 80 consistent with severe PTSD symptoms, K10 score 32, recent FBC and TFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment recommendation?

options.text: Oral prazosin 1 mg at night for nightmares without other adjunctive psychological or pharmacological therapy
options.rationale: Prazosin is an adjunct for trauma nightmares once first-line therapy is established and is not used as monotherapy for global PTSD symptoms. (Source: ASTSS PTSD guideline)

options.text: Oral sertraline 50 mg daily titrated up to 200 mg daily as the sole initial intervention without therapy
options.rationale: SSRIs are second-line in PTSD after psychological therapies and are added when trauma-focused therapy is unavailable, declined or insufficient. (Source: ASTSS PTSD guideline)

options.text: Oral diazepam 5 mg three times daily for symptomatic control of anxiety and intrusive trauma symptoms
options.rationale: Long-term benzodiazepines worsen PTSD outcomes by impeding fear extinction and are explicitly discouraged. (Source: ASTSS PTSD guideline)

options.text: Trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing as first-line therapy
options.rationale: Australian guidance places trauma-focused psychological therapies including TF-CBT and EMDR ahead of pharmacotherapy as first-line treatment for adult PTSD with adequate-intensity symptoms. (Source: ASTSS PTSD guideline; RANZCP: PTSD)

options.text: Oral mirtazapine 30 mg at night as initial monotherapy for combined anxiety and sleep symptoms in PTSD
options.rationale: Mirtazapine has limited evidence in PTSD and is not preferred over established SSRIs when pharmacotherapy is selected. (Source: ASTSS PTSD guideline)

explanation.summary: Adult PTSD with adequate-intensity symptoms is treated first-line with trauma-focused psychological therapy, either TF-CBT or EMDR delivered over 8 to 12 sessions. SSRIs (sertraline or paroxetine) are second-line and may be combined with therapy. Benzodiazepines are contraindicated long-term because they impair fear extinction and worsen long-term symptoms. Adjuncts such as prazosin can target persistent trauma nightmares.
key_points: First-line PTSD therapy is TF-CBT or EMDR over 8 to 12 sessions.
Sertraline or paroxetine are second-line when therapy is unavailable or insufficient.
Benzodiazepines worsen PTSD long-term and are avoided.
explanation.pearls: Offer TF-CBT or EMDR as first-line for PTSD with significant symptoms; sertraline 50 mg daily titrating to 200 mg is the second-line pharmacological choice.

subtopic_detail: ECT authorisation for a detained patient who refuses
stem: You are the psychiatry registrar in a NSW mental health facility. A 68-year-old woman detained with psychotic depression has nihilistic delusions, refuses food and fluids, and has a BMI of 16. Two adequate antidepressant trials have failed; she responded to ECT previously. She refuses ECT, saying she does not deserve treatment. Her family supports it.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 108/68, HR 64, BMI 16, T 36.4 degrees C, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Investigations: FBC, U&E, LFT and ECG normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate way to proceed with ECT?

options.text: Proceed on her family's verbal consent because her illness removes insight
options.rationale: Under the NSW Mental Health Act 2007 no relative, designated carer or principal care provider can consent to ECT. Consent comes from the patient or, failing that, from the Mental Health Review Tribunal. (Source: NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: electro convulsive therapy)
source_refs: NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: electro convulsive therapy

options.text: Continue antidepressant titration and defer ECT despite her worsening refusal
options.rationale: Two adequate trials have failed while she starves. Deferring definitive treatment in psychotic depression with food refusal and a prior ECT response risks death by inanition. (Source: RANZCP Position Statement on ECT)

options.text: Apply to the Mental Health Review Tribunal for an ECT administration inquiry
options.rationale: For a detained or involuntary patient the authorised medical officer must apply to the Tribunal. The Tribunal first decides whether she can give informed consent and has given it; if she cannot consent, or can but refuses, it then decides whether ECT is reasonable and proper and necessary or desirable for her safety or welfare, on certificates from two medical practitioners, at least one a psychiatrist. (Source: NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: electro convulsive therapy)
source_refs: NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: electro convulsive therapy

options.text: Refer to the NCAT Guardianship Division for substitute consent to ECT
options.rationale: The Guardianship Division consents to other medical and dental treatment for an adult without capacity. ECT for a person detained under the Mental Health Act 2007 sits with the Mental Health Review Tribunal instead. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007)

options.text: Give ECT under emergency duty of care without any further legal process
options.rationale: Duty of care covers immediate physical emergencies. The Act provides no route to a planned course of ECT that bypasses the Tribunal, and unlawful administration of ECT carries civil and criminal penalties. (Source: NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: electro convulsive therapy)
source_refs: NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: electro convulsive therapy

explanation.summary: In NSW, ECT for an involuntary or detained patient requires an ECT administration inquiry before the Mental Health Review Tribunal. The Tribunal determines capacity to give informed consent, and where the person cannot consent, refuses, or neither consents nor refuses, it determines whether ECT is a reasonable and proper treatment that is necessary or desirable for the person's safety or welfare. Two medical practitioners, at least one a psychiatrist, must certify that opinion. Family consent has no legal standing, although designated carers and the principal care provider must be notified of the application.
key_points: Detained or involuntary patient plus proposed ECT equals an application to the Tribunal.
Two medical practitioners must certify, at least one a psychiatrist.
A determination lasts 6 months and ordinarily covers up to 12 treatments.
No relative or carer can consent to ECT for an adult in NSW.
explanation.pearls: Severe melancholic depression with food refusal carries a high short-term mortality, so say so in the application: the Tribunal can list an urgent ECT inquiry outside its usual fortnightly sitting when the physical risk is documented.

sources.label: NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: electro convulsive therapy

subtopic_detail: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose with QRS widening
stem: You are the emergency department registrar called to a 22-year-old woman brought in 90 minutes after ingesting 60 of her grandmother's amitriptyline 25 mg tablets. She is now drowsy with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 11. The paramedics have placed an intravenous cannula. There are no co-ingestants identified. She is otherwise well with no chronic disease.

data_table.Vital signs: T 35.9 °C, HR 124, BP 92/56, RR 22, SpO2 96% room air
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, dilated pupils, dry mucous membranes, hypoactive bowel sounds, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: ECG: sinus tachycardia 124, QRS 132 ms, terminal R wave in aVR 4 mm. VBG: pH 7.30, pCO2 32 mmHg, HCO3 17 mmol/L, lactate 3.4 mmol/L. Na 137, K 3.4 mmol/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 8.4% 1 to 2 mmol/kg as a slow bolus targeting QRS narrowing and arterial pH between 7.45 and 7.55, with intubation if airway protection deteriorates
options.rationale: QRS at or above 100 ms with hypotension and a positive aVR R wave indicates cardiotoxicity from sodium channel blockade; hypertonic sodium bicarbonate overcomes this and is the time-critical intervention. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Start a continuous noradrenaline infusion at 0.1 microgram/kg/min and titrate up to maintain a mean arterial pressure above 65 mmHg without giving any specific sodium channel agent
options.rationale: Vasopressors may be required as an adjunct, but sodium bicarbonate is first-line to address sodium channel blockade and QRS prolongation directly; vasopressors alone do not correct conduction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Administer 50 g of oral activated charcoal slurry via nasogastric tube and admit for observation, deferring intravenous antidote until the patient stabilises clinically over the next hour
options.rationale: Activated charcoal at 90 minutes post-ingestion has limited value, particularly in a drowsy patient with airway risk; bicarbonate must not be deferred for adjunct gastrointestinal decontamination. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Administer intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg increments up to a maximum of 1 mg to reverse the reduced consciousness and re-evaluate the cardiotoxicity after she becomes more alert
options.rationale: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not tricyclic toxicity, and may precipitate seizures in mixed overdoses, worsening acidosis and cardiotoxicity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Give intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g bolus and amiodarone 150 mg over 10 minutes to address the tachycardia and prevent ventricular tachyarrhythmia in a patient with tricyclic toxicity
options.rationale: Class IA, IC and III antiarrhythmics are contraindicated in tricyclic toxicity because they worsen sodium channel blockade; magnesium and amiodarone are not first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose causes cardiotoxicity through sodium channel blockade, anticholinergic effects, and alpha blockade. The triad of QRS prolongation, hypotension and reduced consciousness is the classical presentation. Hypertonic sodium bicarbonate is the time-critical intervention because it overcomes sodium channel blockade through both sodium loading and alkalinisation. Lipid emulsion therapy is considered in refractory cardiotoxicity. Class IA, IC and III antiarrhythmics are contraindicated because they exacerbate conduction block.
key_points: QRS at or above 100 ms predicts seizure and at or above 160 ms predicts ventricular dysrhythmia
A terminal R wave in aVR above 3 mm is a sensitive marker of sodium channel blockade
Hypertonic sodium bicarbonate targeting arterial pH 7.45 to 7.55 narrows QRS
Class IA, IC and III antiarrhythmics are contraindicated and worsen conduction block
Intravenous lipid emulsion is considered for refractory cardiotoxicity
explanation.pearls: Hyperventilation alone after intubation can briefly reverse cardiotoxicity by raising arterial pH; this is a temporising measure while preparing sodium bicarbonate boluses.

stem: A 48-year-old man presents to his GP requesting help to quit smoking. He smokes 25 cigarettes per day and has smoked since age 16. He has tried nicotine patches twice in the past but relapsed within 2 weeks each time. He has a stable history of mild depression managed with sertraline 50 mg daily for 3 years. He has no history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, or seizures. He is motivated to quit and has set a target quit date in 2 weeks.

data_table.Examination: BMI 27, no acute distress, PHQ-9 score 4 (minimal depression)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate smoking cessation pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Nicotine patch 21 mg daily alone with a structured 12-week tapering plan
options.rationale: This patient has already failed two attempts with nicotine patches as monotherapy. Repeating the same intervention is unlikely to succeed. Varenicline has superior efficacy to NRT monotherapy in clinical trials and is appropriate after NRT failure. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction)

options.text: Bupropion sustained-release 150 mg daily for 3 days then 150 mg twice daily
options.rationale: Bupropion is a reasonable option for smoking cessation but has lower efficacy than varenicline in head-to-head trials (EAGLES study). Given two prior NRT failures, the most effective available agent should be offered. Bupropion would be appropriate if varenicline were contraindicated. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines; EAGLES trial)

options.text: Varenicline 0.5 mg daily for 3 days, then 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days, then 1 mg twice daily
options.rationale: Varenicline is the most effective single-agent smoking cessation pharmacotherapy, with quit rates approximately 2-3 times placebo. The standard titration (0.5 mg daily for days 1-3, 0.5 mg twice daily for days 4-7, then 1 mg twice daily from day 8) is started 1-2 weeks before the target quit date. The EAGLES trial confirmed no increased neuropsychiatric risk in patients with stable psychiatric conditions. Sertraline interaction is minimal. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction; EAGLES trial)

options.text: Combination NRT with 21 mg patch plus 4 mg nicotine gum for breakthrough cravings
options.rationale: Combination NRT (patch plus short-acting form) achieves quit rates approaching varenicline and is a reasonable alternative. However, this patient has failed NRT patches twice and may have developed a negative association with NRT. Varenicline offers a different mechanism of action (partial nicotinic agonist) and higher individual efficacy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction; RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)

options.text: Nortriptyline 25 mg nocte titrated to 75 mg daily as a second-line cessation aid
options.rationale: Nortriptyline is a second-line option for smoking cessation, used when first-line agents are contraindicated or have failed. It carries anticholinergic side effects and requires ECG monitoring. Given that first-line options with superior evidence remain available, nortriptyline is premature at this stage. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction; AMH)

explanation.summary: Varenicline is the most effective single-agent smoking cessation pharmacotherapy, acting as a partial agonist at alpha-4-beta-2 nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. It reduces both the reward from smoking and withdrawal symptoms. The EAGLES trial (8144 participants) resolved safety concerns by demonstrating no increased neuropsychiatric adverse events compared with NRT, bupropion, or placebo in patients with and without psychiatric illness. A standard 12-week course is recommended, with extension to 24 weeks for those at high relapse risk.
key_points: Varenicline has the highest single-agent efficacy for smoking cessation
EAGLES trial confirmed neuropsychiatric safety in patients with stable psychiatric illness
Standard titration over the first week reduces nausea (most common side effect)
PBS-subsidised in Australia for one course per 12 months
explanation.pearls: Varenicline achieves continuous abstinence rates of approximately 44% at weeks 9-12 versus 18% for placebo, and the EAGLES trial (2016) led to the removal of the FDA black box warning for neuropsychiatric events.

subtopic_detail: Family-based treatment for adolescent anorexia nervosa
stem: A 15-year-old girl is diagnosed with anorexia nervosa. She has lost 8 kg over 6 months and her BMI is 16.2 kg/m2. She is medically stable with normal vital signs and electrolytes. She lives with both parents and a younger sibling. She is resistant to eating but her parents are engaged and motivated. This is her first eating disorder presentation.

data_table.Investigations: Na+ 140, K+ 3.8, Mg2+ 0.85, phosphate 1.1, ECG normal sinus bradycardia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line outpatient treatment?

options.text: Individual CBT-E with the adolescent focusing on dietary self-monitoring
options.rationale: CBT-E is evidence-based for adults but NOT first-line for adolescent anorexia nervosa. Family-based treatment has the strongest evidence in this age group. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Eating Disorders)

options.text: Fluoxetine 20 mg daily with dietary counselling from a dietitian alone
options.rationale: SSRIs have no evidence base for anorexia nervosa treatment. A dietitian is part of the team but counselling alone is insufficient. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Eating Disorders)

options.text: Family-based treatment (Maudsley approach) with the parents managing refeeding
options.rationale: FBT is the strongest evidence-based treatment for adolescent AN. Phase 1: parents take control of eating; Phase 2: gradual return of autonomy; Phase 3: broader developmental issues. FBT achieves remission in 40-50% by end of treatment. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Eating Disorders)

options.text: Inpatient admission for supervised refeeding with nasogastric supplementation
options.rationale: This patient is medically stable. Inpatient admission is reserved for medical instability (severe bradycardia below 50, electrolyte derangement, hypothermia). First-line outpatient treatment should be attempted first. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Eating Disorders)

options.text: Adolescent-focused psychodynamic therapy with fortnightly family sessions
options.rationale: AFT has some evidence but is less effective than FBT in head-to-head trials. With engaged parents, FBT is clearly the first choice. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Eating Disorders)

explanation.summary: FBT is the gold-standard outpatient treatment for adolescent AN. It externalises the illness, removes blame, and empowers parents to manage refeeding. SSRIs have no role in AN treatment.
key_points: FBT is first-line for adolescent AN per RANZCP and NICE guidelines
FBT externalises the illness and empowers parents
SSRIs have no evidence base for AN
Inpatient admission is reserved for medical instability
explanation.pearls: FBT achieves full remission in 40-50% of adolescents at end of treatment, with 75% in full remission at 5-year follow-up in the original Maudsley trial.

stem:
A 24-year-old woman with a 2-year history of bipolar I disorder is admitted from home after 5 days of progressive immobility, mutism, food refusal and posturing in unusual positions held for hours. She was last manic 6 months ago and was prescribed olanzapine and lithium, which her mother says she may not have taken for 3 weeks. There is no fever and no muscular rigidity.

Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale (BFCRS) score is 18, with stupor, mutism, posturing, immobility and waxy flexibility. There are no focal neurological signs. Routine bloods show creatinine kinase 220 U/L (mild rise), white cells 9.4 x10^9/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 122/78, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Mute, postural maintenance with passive limb positioning, no rigidity, no rash, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: FBC and CMP unremarkable except CK 220, TFTs normal, urine drug screen negative, CT brain normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: IV lorazepam 2 mg challenge and reassess BFCRS at 5 to 10 minutes
options.rationale: A lorazepam challenge (1 to 2 mg IV with reassessment of catatonia signs at 5 to 10 minutes) is both diagnostic and therapeutic; a positive response supports the diagnosis and guides regular benzodiazepine treatment. (Source: BAP Catatonia Guidelines; eTG Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence high-dose IV haloperidol 10 mg as urgent treatment
options.rationale: Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and risk transition to neuroleptic malignant syndrome; antipsychotics should be paused or switched while catatonia is treated. (Source: BAP Catatonia Guidelines)

options.text: Restart oral lithium 600 mg twice daily and observe for 48 hours
options.rationale: Restarting the mood stabiliser may help her bipolar illness later, but does not address the acute catatonic state which requires benzodiazepine challenge and possibly ECT. (Source: BAP Catatonia Guidelines)

options.text: Administer IM ziprasidone 20 mg and IM diphenhydramine 50 mg
options.rationale: Acute behavioural disturbance protocols do not apply; she is mute and immobile not agitated, and IM antipsychotic risks NMS in catatonia. (Source: BAP Catatonia Guidelines)

options.text: Proceed directly to ECT after Mental Health Act assessment
options.rationale: ECT is the most effective treatment for catatonia, but a lorazepam challenge is the standard first step; ECT is escalated to when lorazepam fails or features of malignant catatonia emerge. (Source: BAP Catatonia Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndrome of motor, behavioural and autonomic disturbance that can complicate mood, psychotic, neurological and general medical disorders. Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale is the standard quantification tool. A lorazepam challenge (1 to 2 mg IV/IM/PO) with reassessment at 5 to 10 minutes is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Responders are continued on regular benzodiazepine (lorazepam 6 to 24 mg/24 hours titrated). Antipsychotics should be paused because of NMS risk. Failure to respond, malignant catatonia (autonomic instability, hyperthermia, rigidity) or rapid deterioration warrants ECT, which has remission rates above 80 percent. Always exclude organic causes (encephalitis, NMDA-receptor encephalitis, metabolic).
key_points: BFCRS quantifies catatonia features
Lorazepam challenge 1 to 2 mg - diagnostic and therapeutic
Pause antipsychotics - risk of NMS
ECT for non-responders or malignant catatonia
Always exclude organic causes (encephalitis, metabolic)
explanation.pearls: A lorazepam challenge of 2 mg IV with BFCRS scored before and at 10 minutes is both diagnostic and the first treatment - a 50 percent reduction in score is a positive response and guides regular benzodiazepine dosing.
